title: From Competition Release to Ecosystem Functioning: Moderate Thinning Regulates Soil Moisture Availability and Vegetation Responses in Restored Semiarid Caragana microphylla Shrublands of the Loess Plateau, China
content:
ABSTRACT

Thinning is widely applied to regulate vegetation density and alleviate competition for soil water availability in restored semiarid shrublands; however, how thinning intensity regulates integrated plant–soil responses and functioning across a thinning gradient remains insufficiently quantified, as previous studies have emphasized vegetation or soil-water responses rather than their integrated responses to thinning intensity. This study evaluated how thinning intensity regulates vegetation growth, soil moisture, understory vegetation and community composition in Caragana microphylla shrublands in the Anjiapo catchment, Zulihe Watershed, western Loess Plateau, China. Field measurements during the 2024–2026 growing seasons quantified shrub traits, soil moisture, biomass, and understory community attributes under four thinning intensities: control (CT, 0%), light thinning (LT, 20%), moderate thinning (MT, 40%) and heavy thinning (HT, 60%). Moderate thinning produced the strongest responses, with the highest plant height, diameter at stump height, basal area and stem volume. Soil moisture reached its maximum under moderate thinning (11.14% ± 1.55%), accompanied by the highest herbaceous biomass (0.22 ± 0.01 t ha−1), shrub biomass (0.24 ± 0.01 t ha−1), herb-layer Shannon diversity (1.66 ± 0.13) and shrub-layer species richness (8.67 ± 0.66). Thinning significantly altered understory community composition, with moderate thinning showing a distinct community position. These findings suggest that moderate thinning may provide a management strategy for balancing vegetation performance and soil water availability, thereby supporting ecohydrological functioning in restored C. microphylla shrublands.
